rows.question: Can a CUDA event that has never been recorded establish successful completion of earlier work? Explain precisely.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Can a CUDA event that has never been recorded establish successful completion of earlier work? Explain precisely.
rows.answer: No. A CUDA event that has never been recorded does not establish completion of earlier work. cudaEventQuery and cudaEventSynchronize can return cudaSuccess for that event because it represents no recorded work—not because earlier work has finished. To establish completion, record the event in the stream after the relevant work, then successfully query or synchronize it; this covers work ordered before that recording, not unrelated work in other streams.

review.note: Never-recorded event success denotes empty work; record after relevant stream operations and qualify unrelated streams.
review.usefulPrefix: No. A CUDA event that has never been recorded does not establish completion of earlier work.

rows.name: context-15
rows.question: A client retries a charge operation after a network timeout. How does a durable idempotency key avoid a duplicate charge, and what must be atomic?
rows.recognizedQuestion: A client retries a charge operation after a network timeout. How does a durable idempotency key avoid a duplicate charge, and what must be atomic?
rows.answer: A durable idempotency key lets the retry identify the same logical charge and return its stored result instead of charging again. The server must atomically claim the key and commit the charge together with the durable outcome, so concurrent retries or a crash cannot leave a charge without its deduplication record. If the charge happens at an external payment provider, a local database transaction is insufficient: pass the same key to a provider that durably enforces idempotency and reconcile uncertain outcomes rather than issuing a new charge.

review.note: Durable idempotent outcome/charge atomicity, concurrent claim and external-provider boundary/reconciliation.
review.usefulPrefix: A durable idempotency key lets the retry identify the same logical charge and return its stored result instead of charging again.

rows.name: context-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout does not tell the client whether the charge succeeded—the response may simply have been lost. Retrying with the same durable key lets the server recognize the operation and return its saved outcome rather than charge again. The charge and its deduplication record must commit atomically, with concurrent attempts for that key serialized; otherwise a crash could leave a charge without a record and allow a duplicate. For an external payment provider, a local transaction cannot guarantee that atomicity: use the same provider-supported idempotency key and reconcile uncertain outcomes.

review.note: Timeout may hide success; charge/dedup atomicity and stable provider key explain retry safety.
review.usefulPrefix: Because a timeout does not tell the client whether the charge succeeded—the response may simply have been lost.

Keeping expectation 3 can cause repeated failures; updating only the expectation while keeping proposal 4 could overwrite the other thread’s progress.

rows.question: Why does a transaction that commits before an external HTTP side effect need an outbox for reliable eventual delivery?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does a transaction that commits before an external HTTP side effect need an outbox for reliable eventual delivery?
rows.answer: An outbox closes the crash gap between committing the transaction and sending the HTTP request. Write the pending request into the outbox atomically with the business changes, so a crash after commit cannot erase the obligation to send it; a worker then retries delivery and durably records success. Delivery is generally at least once, so the receiver needs an idempotency key to prevent duplicate effects if the request succeeds but its acknowledgment is lost.

review.note: Atomic durable outbox closes commit/send gap; at-least-once effects require receiver idempotency.
review.usefulPrefix: An outbox closes the crash gap between committing the transaction and sending the HTTP request.

rows.name: context-28
rows.question: Actually switch to database isolation. Explain the difference between snapshot isolation and serializability with a concrete write-skew example.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Actually switch to database isolation. Explain the difference between snapshot isolation and serializability with a concrete write-skew example.
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot, but it can still allow write skew; serializability guarantees an outcome equivalent to running transactions one at a time.

Suppose Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain on call. Two concurrent transactions each read that both are on call: one takes Alice off call, while the other takes Bob off call. Under snapshot isolation, they update different rows, so both can commit, leaving nobody on call—even though each transaction saw someone else available.

Under serializable isolation, both cannot commit with that outcome: whichever transaction logically runs second must see only one person on call and leave them on call. The database must prevent the conflicting execution, for example by aborting one transaction for retry.

review.note: Concrete two-doctor disjoint-row snapshot write skew violates invariant; serializable equivalent order prevents both off.
review.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot, but it can still allow write skew; serializability guarantees an outcome equivalent to running transactions one at a time.

rows.name: context-29
rows.question: Correction: use a single atomic transaction for the entire read-check-write invariant. Does that alone guarantee serializability under snapshot isolation?

rows.answer: No. Making each read-check-write operation one atomic transaction does not make snapshot isolation serializable. Alice’s and Bob’s transactions can each read a snapshot showing both on call, pass the check, and update different rows; both can commit because their writes do not conflict, leaving nobody on call. Atomicity prevents partial commits, not write skew; use serializable isolation or a shared locking/conflict mechanism that protects the invariant.

review.note: Whole read-check-write transaction atomicity alone does not protect cross-row invariant under SI.
review.usefulPrefix: No. Making each read-check-write operation one atomic transaction does not make snapshot isolation serializable.

rows.name: context-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing changes, not that concurrent transactions behave as if run sequentially. Starting with Alice and Bob both on call, each transaction reads that snapshot, checks that the other person is on call, and takes its own person off call; under snapshot isolation, both can commit because they write different rows. Nobody remains on call, whereas in either serial order the second transaction would see only one person on call and refuse the update—so the result is not serializable.

review.note: Causal all-or-nothing versus serial order explanation; concrete snapshots/both off incompatible with either serial order.
review.usefulPrefix: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing changes, not that concurrent transactions behave as if run sequentially.
